data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a rational choice based on 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) rather than probability, accepting the cost that verisimilitude remains a regulative ideal without a formal calculus.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd/Miller proof that verisimilitude is undefined in deterministic frameworks holds universally, this defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory logically entails assigning it higher subjective probability, the distinction fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between logical probability (which decreases with content) and corroboration (which reports past performance). The preference for acting on the best-tested theory is a methodological rule to select the theory with the highest potential verisimilitude, acknowledging it might still be false.
